stories.headline: Francis Halzen wins physics Nobel for IceCube neutrino observatory
stories.dek: The prize honors the South Pole detector that found high-energy neutrinos arriving from deep space through Antarctic ice.
paragraphs: Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel prize in physics for leading the IceCube neutrino observatory at the South Pole. The Nobel committee cited his role in building the detector and in the 2013 discovery of high-energy neutrinos from beyond Earth. The award was announced on Tuesday.

Neutrinos are tiny particles that pass through planets, buildings and people with almost no interaction. IceCube detects the rare cases when one hits atomic matter and creates a faint flash of light. To do that, researchers placed thousands of light sensors deep inside a cubic kilometre of clear Antarctic ice.

The prize recognizes one breakthrough, but neutrino astronomy is still young. Scientists are still trying to trace more of these particles back to their sources and to build larger or better detectors. Halzen said he hopes the Nobel will help support a new proposal for future work.
stories.changes: For readers, this means astronomy now includes another way to study the universe, not just light and gravitational waves.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean neutrinos are about to change daily life, deliver messages from aliens, or replace existing telescopes.

cover.title: Nobel prize honors South Pole detector that found cosmic neutrinos
cover.standfirst: The 2026 physics Nobel goes to Francis Halzen for leading IceCube, a vast detector built into Antarctic ice at the South Pole. It first identified high-energy neutrinos from deep space in 2013. Scientists now hope to trace more of these particles to violent cosmic sources.

art.label: Decorative flat
art.concept: Show a full-cover field of Antarctic ice in flat layered blue bands, pierced from the top by a strict grid of vertical IceCube strings made of identical dark round modules, repeated edge to edge. Break that order with one single diagonal chain of modules flaring in a hot accent colour, stepping dot-to-dot through the array as a neutrino event races across the detector; on the snow surface above, reduce the South Pole station to a tiny unmistakable cluster of low buildings and one minute bundled figure turning toward the lit line. Keep the lower third quieter by letting the glowing chain fade out before the bottom, leaving broad calm ice bands for type.
art.note: Quiet, crisp, scientific; icy blues, white, and a small electric violet flash.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a beautiful broken pattern; a beat later you realise the one impossible lit diagonal is the deep-space neutrino being caught inside the buried South Pole observatory.

stories.headline: Kenya confirms first Ebola case after traveler dies in Nairobi
stories.dek: The man had traveled from eastern Congo through Uganda and passed airport screening before relatives took him to hospital.
paragraphs: Kenya said on Tuesday that it has confirmed its first ever Ebola case after a Kenyan citizen died in Nairobi. The announcement came after lab tests on a man who had recently returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where a large outbreak is still spreading.

Officials said the man had been ill for about a month before traveling by road to Kampala and then flying to Nairobi on Saturday. He was admitted to Nairobi Hospital with fever, chills and bleeding under the skin. Health authorities say medicine may have hidden his symptoms during airport screening.

The main unknown is whether the virus spread before he was isolated. Kenya has identified 28 contacts, including relatives and health workers, and is tracing 23 passengers and four crew members from his flight. The outbreak in Congo involves the Bundibugyo strain, which has no proven vaccine or treatment yet.

cover.title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case after traveler dies in Nairobi
cover.standfirst: The man had traveled from eastern Congo through Uganda and passed airport screening before relatives took him to hospital.

art.label: Maximalist doodle
art.concept: A single walk-through airport fever-screening arch sits slightly above centre, drawn as one continuous maximalist doodle silhouette and split by state, not by a hard line. On the left, only a few calm transit items pass neatly through it — a jacket, carry-on bag, shoes, passport pages and blister packs — while on the right that same passage has visibly given way into consequence: latex gloves, sample vials, a stethoscope, IV tubing, seat-belt buckles, a house keyring, a cooking pot lid and a hospital wristband fan outward from the arch as if one missed crossing has propagated from airport to home to ward; keep the lower third largely open white for type.
art.second_beat: First you see a screening gate; a beat later you realise the objects have shifted from travel to household to clinical, telling the whole missed-screening chain in one image.

stories.headline: Drone strike sinks cargo ship off Bulgaria and crew goes missing
stories.dek: Two merchant ships were hit in Bulgaria's Black Sea zone, and rescuers are searching for the crew of a sunken Togo-flagged vessel.
paragraphs: A merchant ship sank in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday after a drone strike, and its crew is missing. Bulgarian officials said two cargo vessels were hit about 70 miles off Byala. One crew was rescued. Authorities are now searching the water for survivors and signs of pollution.

The attack appears to be the first reported strike on merchant shipping in Bulgarian waters since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. Maritime security monitors named the vessels as the Togo-flagged ALFA WATAN and the Palau-flagged ABLE. Bulgaria said the rescued ship was carrying grain and two people were injured.

It is still not officially confirmed who carried out the strike, though a maritime security source said early assessments pointed to Russia. The cargo on the sunken ship has not been disclosed. Officials have not said how many crew are missing, or whether fuel or cargo has leaked into the sea.
stories.changes: For people around the Black Sea, the war now looks closer to civilian shipping routes and coastal trade.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean commercial shipping across the whole Black Sea has stopped or that Bulgaria is entering the war.

cover.title: Drone strike sinks cargo ship off Bulgaria and crew is missing
cover.standfirst: Two merchant ships were hit on Tuesday in Bulgaria's Black Sea economic zone, about 70 miles off Byala. One grain ship's crew was rescued with two injured. A second vessel sank, and rescuers are searching for its missing crew and any sign of pollution.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: A towering Black Sea wave fills the frame, engraved almost black with tight white burin lines, its mass rearing from left to right. At the crest, a small merchant cargo ship is caught stern-down and tipping into the trough, already half-lost; inside the white hollow of the curling breaker, the negative space cleanly resolves into the silhouette of a diving military drone, nose aimed at the ship. Keep the lower third comparatively open as dark water and trough, so type can sit across it without fighting detail.
art.note: Cold, muted blues and greys; quiet, tense, and spare.
art.second_beat: First you see a ship going under in violent sea; a beat later the wave’s white hollow reveals the drone shape, so the sea itself becomes the strike.

stories.headline: Russia says it downed nearly 900 Ukrainian drones overnight
stories.dek: Moscow said the attack killed two people, while reports said a fuel depot in the Moscow region caught fire.
paragraphs: Russia said its air defences shot down nearly 900 Ukrainian drones overnight across several regions, occupied Crimea and the Sea of Azov. Moscow's mayor said hundreds were aimed at the capital region. The claimed scale matters because Ukraine is pressing deeper strikes on Russian fuel and transport targets.

Ukraine has built longer-range drones and missiles during the war, allowing it to hit Russian territory despite Russia's larger air force. Ukrainian forces have repeatedly targeted refineries and fuel depots, saying they want to disrupt supplies for the war. Russia has also kept striking Ukrainian cities, bridges and Black Sea ports.

Many key claims remain unverified, including the full number of drones, the extent of damage and Ukraine's past claim that it disabled 51% of Russia's refining capacity. It is also unclear how long Russia can protect fuel sites at this pace, or whether these attacks will change battlefield positions soon.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means the war is reaching deeper into Russian infrastructure and can still affect fuel prices and trade far beyond the front.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Russia has lost control of its airspace or that either side is close to ending the war.

cover.title: Russia says it shot down nearly 900 Ukrainian drones
cover.standfirst: Russia said its air defences intercepted almost 900 Ukrainian drones overnight across multiple regions, Crimea and the Sea of Azov. Moscow officials said hundreds were aimed at the capital region, and reports said a fuel depot near Moscow burned. The full damage is still unclear.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: A black night sky fills almost edge to edge with a dense diagonal swarm of tiny identical drone silhouettes driving toward Moscow, so numerous they begin to read like a storm front rather than individual machines. Near the upper field, keep the Kremlin/Moscow skyline as a small, unmistakable silhouette under pressure; in the Moscow-region foreground, only one break in the pattern: a single drone has become a red-orange fireball erupting from a circular fuel tank farm, the lone point where the abstract mass resolves into visible damage. Keep the lower third mostly quiet and dark, with the depot and blast sitting just above it so cover lines can sit cleanly beneath.
art.note: Grave and stark, with black, ash grey and one hard orange-red flame.
art.second_beat: First you see an overwhelming swarm; a beat later you realise only one drone has changed shape, and that single rupture turns statistics into an inevitable hit on a fuel depot near Moscow.

stories.headline: Francis Halzen wins physics Nobel for neutrino observatory work
stories.dek: The prize honors work on IceCube, a detector buried in Antarctic ice that traced high-energy neutrinos back to space.
paragraphs: Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday. The prize cites his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from astrophysical sources. The award was announced in Stockholm as this year's Nobel prizes are unveiled.

Neutrinos are tiny particles with almost no mass and no electric charge. They pass through matter so easily that billions move through every person each second. IceCube, built deep in Antarctic ice, detects rare flashes of light when a neutrino hits an atom, letting scientists infer where in space it came from.

The Nobel citation honors a method and a discovery, not a final answer about the universe's most violent engines. Scientists still debate which objects produce the highest-energy neutrinos and how. The prize also leaves open a familiar question in big science: how much credit belongs to one person in a vast international collaboration.
stories.changes: For readers, this puts neutrinos and the Antarctic detector that found them into the small set of discoveries judged to have changed physics.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean neutrinos are newly discovered, dangerous, or about to produce everyday technology.

cover.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize for finding cosmic neutrinos
cover.standfirst: The 2026 physics Nobel Prize goes to Francis Halzen for work on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica. The award cites the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from astrophysical sources, particles that help scientists trace violent events deep in space. More detail on the research will follow this week.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat acid-green ground, place a stark black silhouette of Antarctica as a chunky ice mass rising from the bottom edge, its lower third kept mostly empty for type. From inside the ice, unmistakable IceCube sensor strings hang in a rigid vertical grid, but the whole embedded array is being absurdly tilted upward like a telescope aimed at a single white starburst in the upper corner; add one crude black marker arrow slashing from the tilted array toward the burst, and nothing else.
art.note: Cold, precise, luminous blues and black with one bright electric accent.
art.second_beat: First you see an impossible glacier using a telescope; then it clicks that the buried IceCube detector is being turned into what it truly became—an observatory in the ice looking back out into space.

stories.headline: Former German spy chief arrested over suspected secret leaks
stories.dek: Prosecutors say August Hanning got about 2,000 BND documents from a former aide and used some material in private consulting work.
paragraphs: German prosecutors arrested former BND chief August Hanning on Tuesday on suspicion of treason, espionage and passing state secrets to a foreign intelligence service. They say the case surfaced now after evidence was found during a separate search of his home in another criminal investigation.

Hanning led Germany's foreign intelligence service from 1998 to 2005. Prosecutors say he and former aide Manfred D. agreed in 2010 that the aide would keep sending valuable BND material to Hanning for payment. They say roughly 2,000 documents were passed on, many marked for internal intelligence briefings.

Prosecutors have not said which foreign service was involved or whether the classified material reached its intended recipient. It is also unclear how long the alleged transfers continued. The allegations have renewed criticism of former senior officials doing private consulting work after leaving posts with top security access.
stories.changes: For readers in Germany, the case may bring tighter rules on what former intelligence officials can do after leaving office.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Germany's intelligence service as a whole was spying for another country or that the accusations are yet proven in court.

cover.title: Germany arrests former intelligence chief over suspected secret leaks
cover.standfirst: German prosecutors arrested former BND chief August Hanning, 80, and a former aide on Tuesday. They say the aide sent him about 2,000 classified documents over years, and that some information was later shared in work linked to a foreign intelligence service. The foreign country has not been named.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat acid-green ground, build a rigid wall-like grid of black-and-white intelligence file folders, all identical, cropped tight so they feel institutional and oppressive. Near the top row, one folder is being pulled halfway out toward us at a sharp angle; from the dark slot behind it, a burst of loose white dossier pages slips and cascades downward, while a single rough black marker circle isolates that breach. Keep the lower third largely empty green, with only a few falling page corners entering it.
art.note: Cold, accusatory, cut-paper look in gray, black and muted red.
art.second_beat: First you see a disciplined archive; then you spot the one file in the act of being stolen, and the whole system suddenly reads as a leak from inside.

stories.headline: Qualcomm agrees to pay Huawei in new patent licensing deal
stories.dek: The companies signed a multi-year cross-license for 5G, AI, compute and networking, and Qualcomm will also buy some Huawei US patents.
paragraphs: Qualcomm said it will pay Huawei under a new multi-year patent cross-license, a sharp change in a relationship where Huawei had long paid Qualcomm. The deal covers 5G, AI, compute and networking patents. Qualcomm will also buy some Huawei patents filed in the United States, pending regulatory approval.

The two companies have licensed patents to each other since 2001, when Huawei took a royalty-bearing license for CDMA equipment. Their ties worsened after Huawei stopped paying Qualcomm royalties in 2018. They settled a back-payment dispute in 2020, and Huawei's earlier license expired by early 2025.

Neither company disclosed the value of the new payments, the number of patents being sold, or when the sale will close. Huawei said the agreement does not include other business cooperation, so it does not reopen chip sales. Regulators still need to clear the patent purchase.
stories.changes: For readers, this shows Huawei is now earning serious money from patents, not just paying other tech companies for them.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Huawei phones will suddenly use Qualcomm chips again, or that US restrictions on Huawei have been lifted.

cover.title: Qualcomm will pay Huawei under a new patent deal
cover.standfirst: Qualcomm and Huawei signed a multi-year cross-license covering 5G, AI, compute and networking patents. Qualcomm will also buy some Huawei US patents after regulatory approval. The companies did not disclose the price, the patent count, or a closing date.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: A single unbranded smartphone lies diagonally on clean seamless paper, shot dead-on like a product still life. From beneath the left edge, a small fan of identical SIM-sized metallic cards is visibly sliding out; at the right edge, an equal fan of the same cards is simultaneously being pulled back under the phone from the opposite direction, so the handset becomes the hinge between two opposite flows. Keep everything else out of frame and leave the lower third empty; the only drama is the mirrored in-and-out motion under one phone.
art.note: Cool, exact, corporate mood; steel gray, white, and muted red.
art.second_beat: First read: money or rights are moving around a phone; second beat: the same kind of cards are going in opposite directions under the same object, making the licensing relationship's reversal instantly legible.

stories.headline: OpenAI rolls out hidden text marks for EU ChatGPT output
stories.dek: The system tweaks word choice to leave a statistical trace, but OpenAI says editing and short passages can break detection.
paragraphs: OpenAI said it will begin marking some AI-written text so it can be identified later, as required by the EU AI Act. In coming weeks, eligible ChatGPT and Codex output in the European Union will carry an invisible watermark. API customers worldwide can opt in starting now for select models.

The watermark, called textGrain, works by steering the model between similar word choices in a hidden pattern. A detector then checks whether that pattern appears in a passage. OpenAI said the method is similar in broad outline to systems other AI companies are also building to meet the same European rules.

The system is far from certain. OpenAI said it can miss marked text and can wrongly flag unmarked text, especially in short passages or rigid subjects like mathematics. Editing also weakens it fast. Replacing 10% of words with synonyms cut detection sharply in tests, and heavier rewriting cut it further.
stories.changes: Readers in the EU may start receiving some ChatGPT and Codex text that carries a hidden marker researchers can test for later.
stories.unchanged: A watermark does not prove a person cheated, does not show who used the tool, and does not tell you whether the text is true.

cover.title: OpenAI adds hidden markers to some ChatGPT text in Europe
cover.standfirst: OpenAI said some ChatGPT and Codex text sent to eligible users in the European Union will soon carry an invisible watermark. API customers can opt in now on select models, but the company says detection can fail on short text and can weaken quickly after editing.

art.label: Minimal mark
art.concept: On a pale ground, place a single small black ink droplet high in the frame, suspended mid-fall and slightly off-centre so the lower third stays empty for type. Cut a clean ChatGPT-knot silhouette out of the droplet itself as negative space — unmistakable on second look, but not oversized — so it reads first as an ordinary ink mark and then as OpenAI embedded inside the mark. Keep everything flat, crisp and minimal: one droplet, one cut-out, no page, no extra symbols.
art.note: Clean, procedural, public-interest mood; EU blue, black, and muted yellow.
art.second_beat: First you see a falling ink mark; then you realise the watermark is hidden inside the mark itself, specifically tying the invisible trace to ChatGPT output.

stories.headline: Asos app sends hack threat to millions of customers
stories.dek: A push alert claimed attackers had compromised Asos data systems and threatened to leak information through a newly created Telegram channel.
paragraphs: Asos customers received a push notification on Tuesday saying the retailer had been hacked and threatening to leak data unless the company engaged with the sender. The message referred to a compromised Snowflake instance, a cloud data platform. Asos's app and website remained online, but the alert triggered immediate concern.

Asos sells clothing online and owns brands including Topshop and Miss Selfridge. It says it has 17 million customers across 150 countries. Cybersecurity specialists said the message was notable because it appeared inside Asos's own app, suggesting some access to company systems, though not proving the full breach claims.

It is still unclear whether any customer data was actually stolen, what information may have been exposed, or how attackers gained access. Experts said customers should avoid links in messages, watch for phishing emails and texts, and change passwords directly through the official website while Asos investigates.
stories.changes: Ordinary Asos customers should treat any follow-up message about passwords, refunds or payment checks as suspicious until the company confirms the facts.
stories.unchanged: This does not yet prove that your personal or payment data has been stolen, and the app warning alone is not evidence of the full breach claimed.

cover.title: Asos app sends customers a message threatening to leak data
cover.standfirst: Asos customers received a push alert on Tuesday saying attackers had compromised the retailer's Snowflake data system and would leak information unless the company engaged. The website and app were still working, but shares fell sharply and the company now faces urgent questions over whether any customer data was actually taken.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: Top-down on a plain cream tabletop: a handmade smartphone in unmistakable Asos app styling lies slightly above centre, leaving the lower third clean for type. From the lit screen, a single long pink felt tongue-push-notification slithers out and curls into real space, caught mid-unfurl; dangling from its tip is a tiny black paper Telegram plane, with visible glue seams and fingerprints so it feels physically made, not slick. Strip everything else away: no extra alerts, no props, just the app itself producing the threat.
art.note: Sharp, uneasy collage in black, white, acid blue and warning red.
art.second_beat: First read: a grotesque alert escaping a phone; second beat: the danger is worse because it is coming from inside Asos’s own app, with Telegram literally attached to the message.

stories.headline: New York declares measles emergency as cases rise from Pennsylvania
stories.dek: The order broadens who can give MMR shots after New York recorded 108 cases and Pennsylvania reported 977.
paragraphs: New York declared a statewide measles emergency on Monday as an outbreak linked to Pennsylvania continued to spread. Governor Kathy Hochul said the order is meant to speed vaccination and testing after New York recorded 108 cases and health officials warned of possible exposure at Philadelphia International Airport.

Measles is one of the most contagious viruses and can cause pneumonia, brain swelling and death. The United States is having its worst measles year since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported by the CDC. Pennsylvania has reported 977 cases and five deaths, with many cases in rural communities.

The emergency order lets registered nurses order measles tests and allows pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as 2. It also tightens reporting rules for MMR shots. Officials are still tracing exposures, especially among infants, pregnant people without immunity, and immunocompromised people who may need treatment after contact.
stories.changes: It may become easier and faster for families in New York to get children vaccinated and tested outside a doctor's office.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean a lockdown, travel ban, or a new vaccine rule for everyone in the state.

cover.title: New York declares measles emergency as outbreak spreads from Pennsylvania
cover.standfirst: Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide emergency after New York logged 108 measles cases and neighboring Pennsylvania reported 977 cases and five deaths. The order lets more health workers give MMR shots and order tests, while officials trace exposures linked to Philadelphia airport.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: A public-health worker’s gloved hand enters from the left, actively pulling a taut red thread from the unmistakable silhouette of an airport departures board with split-flap rows and a plane-tail visible beyond it. The thread runs diagonally across the image into New York, snagging in three clean, specific places: the wheel of a stroller, a raised rural mailbox on a post, and a black iron fire escape; keep the lower third mostly open and quiet, with the thread doing the storytelling against a pale gouache ground. No words, no map labels — just the act of the line being drawn and caught as it moves from air travel into family, rural, and city life.
art.note: Calm but urgent; clean clinic colors with muted reds and pale blues.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a route line from airport to New York; a beat later, the snags reveal it as a chain of exposures spreading through specific kinds of communities.
